newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Water, a scarce resource, is key to food crisis.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Water, a scarce resource, is key to food crisis.

text.p: Without water, an increasingly scarce and sought-after commodity, there can be no food. This fact is undisputable.
But with more and more mouths to feed, farmers are under pressure to increase production -- and how else to do this but use more water?
The dilemma is one of the more pressing issues to be discussed at the World Food Summit, which will bring together some 100 heads of state and government in Rome next week.

Water experts at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) gave this dire warning in a technical paper prepared for the summit: "It is clear that human demands are about to collide with the ability of the hydrological cycle to supply water".
In simpler terms: Water is becoming globally scarce.
They are talking about fresh water sources, such as rivers, lakes and acquifers, which are tapped not only for agriculture but for drinking, sanitation and industries.

These water sources, finite in nature and dwindling as pollution takes it toll, are more in demand as the world's population, now at 5.8 billion, grows. FAO says it expects there to be three billion more people by the year 2030.
FAO experts recommend increasing the area of farm land through efficient and environmentally-friendly irrigation, noting that more than half of all agriculture production is still rain-fed.
"There are low-income nations who don't have money to import food," said Arumugan Kandiah, a senior officer of FAO's Land and Water Development Division.
"This is the context in which we think water development is important because depending on rain for water for agriculture can cause problems."
In some cases, such as Jordan and Yemen, it is not possible.

"In arid countries, as the population increases, the amount of water they have per person goes down," said Wulf Klohn, FAO senior water resources officer. "In some countries a crisis is arising in that they have no other resources, they have no money. In Yemen and Jordan it's very critical."

Scarce water also has political ramifications as different countries compete for the same sources. This is most evident in the Middle East where water rights are a key negotiating point in ongoing peace talks.
The experts see more potential for "water development" -- their word for irrigation -- in Africa, where some 200 million of the world's 840 million undernourished people live.

"In Africa we have more or less 12 million hectares (30 million acres) of irrigated land," said Jean-Marc Faures, another water resources officer. "We estimate full potential in Africa at 40 million hectares. In a word, they are underusing their resources."

Faures pointed out that the use of irrigation varied immensely in areas of Africa. Northern countries like Egypt used it successfully, tapping into the Nile for centuries, while poorer countries in the south lagged far behind.
FAO research shows that Egypt has 99 percent of its arable land under irrigation while Zaire, currently gripped by ethnic strife, has only 0.2 percent.
But how will these farmers pay for irrigation, whose infrastructure is expensive to buy, install and maintain?
Kandiah said irrigation equipment had to be made cheaper so small farmers could afford it. He also suggested projects in which a group of farmers joined together to share a system.

"Especially in sub-Saharan Africa, you can't just drop in a big-scale project and expect them to perform. We think probably small-scale irrigation is better because it is less expensive and it allows community participation," Kandiah said.
Faures said subsistence farmers, those who grow only what they eat, also had to expand their yield with crops to sell.
"Irrigation has a cost and with subsistence farming you can not pay for that cost," he said. "If irrigation is going to have a future there have to be markets."
He took encouragement from vegetable farmers who in recent years had started successful businesses on the fringes of large African cities. "They can get cash for their crops".
The question remains how farmers will find water for irrigation -- and the answer seems to lie with innovation and technology.
Kandiah says farmers could possibly use more treated urban waste water for irrigation, while richer countries might increase the use for drinking of desalinated water, still a very expensive process.
FAO also advocates the development of more efficient irrigation systems and the reclamation of some 10 million hectares of waterlogged and salinised land.
"What we are concerned about is that there is a big food production gap at the moment...and it will be difficult to close that gap if we do agriculture business as usual," Kandiah said.
